Introduction - December 2011 











#### **Eurozone woes continue to weigh on sentiment and prices** 

Base metals markets have remained under pressure as Eurozone debt issues have persisted and intensified.  Once the threat of a Greek referendum had been avoided, financial markets turned their attention to Italian debt problems and the focus has now encompassed the “AAA” nations within the single-currency.  This has pressured the Euro and the threat to not only E

uropean, but wider, industrial demand, has served to increase consumer caution.  This, in turn, has led to increasing reports of destocking and just-in-time purchasing. 

Prices continue to be volatile, broadly in line with developments in Europe and market perceptions of the potential financial and economic impacts.  Furthermore, growth prospects in most major nations have been revised downwards in recent weeks and months; for example, US Q3 GDP was lowered to 2.0% from the previously released estimate of 2.5%. 

##### **Recent performance amongst metals has been mixed,** 

lead-acid battery manufacturers in China may be slowly ramping up production.  We remain positive on the lead market’s prospects over the medium term, relative to many other base metals. 

Although copper prices have been on a declining trend over the last month or so, there has been considerable volatility around this.  As the designated “macro” metal, Dr Copper’s twists and turns have largely vacillated along with the newsflow from the Eurozone in particular.  Nevertheless, copper has so far remained above the lows seen at the beginning of October, during LME Week.  The well known structural issues remain on the supply-side, and are compounded by ongoing risks related to strikes and weather. However, the demand side of the equation is coming more to the fore as growth estimates are slowing globally and as consumer sentiment stalls and purchasing slows.  Whilst Chinese consumption remains robust, performance is patchy elsewhere.  This has been highlighted by Codelco’s annual premium offers for 2012, which are lower than this year. 

##### **but overall trend has been downward** 

Following a 9.9% fall in October, the Thomson Reuters GFMS Base Metals Index (which is an average of all the base metals) fell a marginal 0.3% in November on a monthly average basis. 

Turning to intra-sector trends, the recent price performance between the LME metals has varied, albeit with a downward bias.  Throughout the recent volatility, lead and zinc prices had, until recently, trended higher since the beginning of November.  However, whilst zinc had subsequently sold off in line with most other base metals, lead had remained relatively supported.  The performance of lead reflects robust demand from the battery sector and a continued decline in exchange stocks. The aluminium market continues to be overshadowed by it’s growing mountain of inventory, but premiums and prices had been supported by ongoing cash-and-carry deals which were tying up the vast majority of this stock in a conducive interest rate environment.  However, consumer destocking has increased and reported stocks have continued to climb, recently surging with the net delivery of 227,000 tonnes in two locations within just a few days, with more expected.  Physical premiums have also come under pressure as producers report slugg

ish purchasing. There have been more power-related production cuts in China, and the aluminium market has become exposed to the risk of a short-covering rally if demand conditions improve and consumers start scrambling for material. Economic Indicators - December 2011 











November ISM index rebounded sharply to 52.7 from 50.8 in the previous month and, positively for the future outlook, the new orders index increased by 4.3 points.  Although it must be remembered that the November ISM was well below the levels seen in the first half of the year, it was notably above the third quarter average of 51. 

Recent indicators have shown an ongoing slowdown in growth in the **Chinese** economy.  IP growth dipped to 12.4% from 13.2% in the previous month, whilst the cumulative growth in fixed asset investment fell to 24.5% in November, from 24.9% over the first ten months.  Furthermore, a disappointing November manufacturing PMI also served to dent sentiment, with the index falling to a 32-month low of 47.7 from 51.0 in the previous month, indicating a sharp deterioration in operating conditions in the sector. 

November vehicle sales confirmed the pick up in the US auto sector and also provide a broad gauge of improving sentiment as consumers commit to “big ticket” purchases. Sales last month on a SAAR basis were 13.6m units, the highest l

evel in over two years. The University of Michigan’s latest survey also points to improving sentiment, with the indicator rising for the fourth month in a row to 66.7. The aforementioned signs have been sufficient to prompt the Chinese government into a shift in monetary stance, with the Central Bank cutting banks’ reserve requirement ratios by 50 basis points in late November. Positively for the industrial metals sector, this move indicates that the government is ready to reverse its previous tightening measures in the face of any significant threats to economic growth. The fall in both consumer and producer price inflation will also allow the government some flexibility to introduce further stimuli to the economy going forward. **Japanese** IP managed to grow by 2.4% month-on-month in October, a robust showing given the ongoing disruptions to component supply following the Thai floods. However, a deterioration in the manufacturing PMI in November, to 49.1, highlights that significant headwinds remain in place. A strengthening yen, supply chain disruptions and the slowdown in exports will all impart restraining influences on IP growth going forward. In the **United States** , whilst third quarter real GDP growth was revised down to 2% (SAAR), from the initial estimate of 2.5%, recent indicators have been encouraging. per. **E2** Aluminium - December 2011 #### **Aluminium** ##### **Recent developments** - **_As Eurozone sovereign debt issues have persisted and deepened, aluminium prices, along with the rest of the base metals complex, have remained under pressure. The cash price hit a recent low of $1,962/tonne and is currently trading around $1,975/tonne._** - **_LME stocks edged higher during November, before two large deliveries in early December (which had been pre-flagged by some market participants) added a net 227,000 tonnes in Vlissingen and Detroit. We had commented last month on reports of off-warrant stock build in some European ports, and this could have been metal simply moved on warrant. Market expectations are for further large deliveries on to the LME._** - **_Generally higher reported stocks have also been concurrent with weakening physical premiums; both reflect a less sanguine demand picture and are in line with producer reports of deteriorating consumer sentiment and increased destocking. Norsk Hydro in Europe, and Novelis in North America, have both raised concerns over the near-term demand outlook. In China, the build in Shanghai exchange stocks may also reflect cautious customer buying, and the government’s recent cut in the reserve ratio of 50 basis points suggests increasing concerns over growth._** ##### **Outlook for the next 12 months** - **_There cannot be any strong degree of clarity over near term price prospects until there is some resolution (or not) to the Eurozone debt problems. Until then, markets are likely to continue remain volatile, but largely rangebound._** - **_As such, our supply/demand outlook remains unchanged for the next twelve months, although downside risks may have heightened. We still see market surpluses in 2011 and 2012 of 638,000 tonnes and 275,000 tonnes, respectively. Consumer destocking and a move towards just-in-time delivery could leave the market vulnerable to a short-covering rally (as could any further significant quantitative easing measures in Europe or the United States). However, we are remaining cautious at the moment for prospects over the next few months. **N2** Nickel & Cobalt - December 2011 China’s exports of stainless flat products fell by just over 30% year on year in October after demand from Taiwan and South Korea fell away sharply. China shipped 100,029 tonnes of stainless flat products in October, compared with 149,190 tonnes in September. Shipments to Taiwan, the major destination for China’s stainless flat products, fell 43.7% month-on-month to 24,647 tonnes, and shipments to South Korea were 48.6% lower at 16,755 tonnes. Imports of stainless flat products in to China fell 7.9% to 54,497 tonnes in October, as imports from Japan fell nearly 20% to 17,643 tonnes. Spot stainless steel prices in China’s Wuxi market have fallen close to a two-year low, due to weak demand and falling nickel prices. ##### **Growth in supply adds to bearish outlook** The bearish longer term argument is the likelihood of a surge in supply after what can be viewed as a near decade-long wait. There appear to be just too many projects for the market to absorb. Also, a number of projects are quite large in relation to the overall size of the nickel market. Other factors which are different this time around include the fact that there are a variety of technologies being employed, and that the bulk of the projects are being commissioned by major mining companies (in sharp contrast to the first generation of HPAL projects). From a market balance perspective, this additional supply is coming at a time of weak demand and prices. Importantly, these will be imposed on a market that has seen both mine and refined output rise by double-digit rates up t

o September. Some of the new capacity is already being ramped up, while others are on the brink of commissioning. Brazil’s Vale will be at the forefront of the likely surge in nickel production with high profile Goro project, which should eventually produce 60,000 tpy of nickel oxide; output is slated at 22,000 tpy this year. Two other operations (ferro-nickel) are currently being ramped up Barro Alto and Onca Puma. Barro Alto will have a capacity to produce 36,000 tpy of ferronickel for more than 32 years. However, it should produce 41,000 tpy in the first five years of operation due to the rich surface ore in the open-pit mine operation. Overall, the company expects to produce 300,000 tonnes of nickel in the full year 2012 compared to 173,000 tonnes up to September 2011. This includes a contribution from its Canadian operations, reflecting the full year operation after the year long strike in 2010/11. **Chinese output surges despite some NPI cutbacks** We are also seeing increases in Chinese primary refined output, which according to the CNIA is currently over 10% higher than year earlier levels and is set to reach 200,000 tonnes for the whole year. The Jinchuan expansion has accounted for the bulk of the growth. NPI output is forecast to be around 260,000 tonnes, although output in the second half of this year will be lower than the first. Although there have been cutbacks, some NPI producers, such as Zhegan and Taiwan-E United, are in the process of raising capacity. It had been thought that falling Chinese domestic nickel pig iron prices would lead to significant further production cuts. Ex-factory prices of high-grade NPI (10-15% Ni) have fallen to RMB 1,290-1,330 per nickel unit ($203-209/nickel unit) from RMB 1,450-1,500/Ni unit in early November. However, stocks of nickel ore are at record levels and imports of nickel ore are still high, which may provide some support to Chinese NPI producers. On a smaller scale, Talvivaara Mining in Finland has confirmed that output should be 16,000 tonnes of nickel this year. It says that 2012 full year production should be in the region of 25,000-30,000 tonnes. The market may also have to have to absorb material from the commissioning of the Ravensthorpe project in Australia, and two projects that have suffered delayed start ups, Ambatovy in Madagascar and Ramu in PNG. ##### **Market outlook** Our market balance and price projections remain unchanged from those detailed in our previous report. We continue to expect zinc prices to average $1,900/tonne over the current quarter, as ongoing macroeconomic concerns continue to impart downward pressure on industrial metals prices. Although our current forecasts for 2012, which show zinc prices averaging $2,250/tonne next year, are unchanged from our previous report, downside risks to our forecasts are intensifying as we near year-end. We will be undertaking a revision of our 2012 forecasts in our January report and it will come of little surprise that, barring any significant improvement in conditions in the Eurozone, any revisions to both our supply demand balance and price projections are expected to paint a more bearish picture for the market than was previously the case. Under our **high case Scenario B,** the Eurozone would recover faster than expected from its current malaise, leading to stronger than expected demand growth and an improvement in investor sentiment towards the industrial metals sector. Under this scenario, prices would be expected to average $2,425/tonne over 2012. In contrast, a further deterioration in conditions in the Eurozone and weaker global demand growth forms the basis for our **low case Scenario C.** Such developments would see the zinc spot price average $1,750/tonne over 2012. Thereafter, our longer term forecasts for the zinc market remain unchanged from our previous report. We expect that the market will struggle to gain significant ground over the first quarter of 2012, weighed down by the ongoing market surplus and economic woes.
